title: Radial-Angular Geometry for Reliable Update Diagnosis in Noisy-Label Learning
claim: Magnitude-based signals confuse hard-clean with noisy samples; comparing update direction against a reference separates them.
layout: 3 colored panels on top, bottom summary strip; left-to-right progression
description: The figure has three rounded, color-tinted panels across the top and a yellow strip along the bottom. Panel A (blue), 'Conventional Signals (Forward Space)', shows a hard clean cat image and a noisy dog image going through a network. Each produces overlapping loss histograms and a 'High Loss' label, so the two cases look alike. Panel B (pink), 'Fisher Geometry (Parameter Space)', shows a heat-map landscape with a blue low-trace region and a red high-trace region. Concentric contour insets are labeled Clean (hard) and Noisy, and a color bar runs from Low to High Fisher trace. Panel C (green), 'Relative Geometric', shows a student network and an EMA teacher network. Angle diagrams of g_obs against g_ref give cos θ≈1 for the hard clean sample and cos θ≪1 for the noisy one, and the output is a trust weight. The bottom strip links magnitude-based signals, then Fisher trace, then direction-based conflict, with formulas for the gradient, trace and conflict C_i.
caption: Overall motivation of RGC. Conventional forward-space signals mainly measure sample difficulty and confuse hard clean samples with noisy samples. Fisher trace moves the signal into parameter space but remains magnitude-based. RGC further compares update directions and helps identify unreliable samples by their directional conflict with a reference update.
abstract: Noisy-label methods often estimate sample reliability from forward-space signals such as loss, confidence, or entropy. These signals indicate whether a sample is difficult to predict, but they do not directly test whether its observed label induces a reliable parameter update. This gap matters because hard clean samples and mislabeled samples can have similar loss while inducing different updates. We recast reliability estimation as diagnosis of the observed-label update. The sample-wise empirical Fisher trace gives a backward-space measure of update energy: for the classifier layer, it factorizes into a prediction-residual term and a feature-sensitivity term, so it captures information beyond scalar loss. Trace, however, is still a radial magnitude signal and cannot decide whether a large update is useful or harmful. We therefore propose Relative Geometric Conflict (RGC), which compares the observed-label gradient with a reference gradient induced by an EMA teacher. The conflict term helps distinguish large but aligned hard-clean updates from large conflicting updates caused by corrupted labels. Across synthetic and real-world noisy-label benchmarks, RGC improves hard-clean preservation and accuracy under our evaluation protocol.
